_note: Undesigned coincidences. Quote verses from the World English Bible (public domain) or keep ESV quotes under ~30 words. Verify each reference before shipping.
sources: Lydia McGrew, Hidden in Plain View: Undesigned Coincidences in the Gospels and Acts (DeWard, 2017)
J. J. Blunt, Undesigned Coincidences in the Writings of the Old and New Testament (1847), public domain

items.question: Why did Jesus ask Philip where to buy bread?

steps.point: Jesus asks Philip, of all people, where to buy bread. John gives no reason.
steps.quote: Jesus therefore, lifting up his eyes and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?”

steps.point: Luke, in his account of the same feeding, says it happened near Bethsaida. Luke never mentions Philip here.
steps.quote: The apostles, when they had returned, told him what things they had done. He took them and withdrew apart to a desert region of a city called Bethsaida.

steps.point: John elsewhere, in passing, says Philip was from Bethsaida.
steps.quote: Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. / These came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee…

steps.point: Put together: Jesus asked the local. Neither author explains this; the explanation only appears when the two are read side by side.

items.question: Why does Mark mention green grass?

steps.point: Mark notes the crowd sat on 'green grass' at the feeding of the 5,000.
steps.quote: He commanded them that everyone should sit down in groups on the green grass.

steps.point: John, independently, says the Passover was near, i.e., spring, the one season Galilee's grass is green.
steps.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.

steps.point: A throwaway color detail in one Gospel matches a calendar note in another.

items.question: Why do the guards say 'Prophesy! Who hit you?'

steps.point: They strike Jesus and say 'Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?' Matthew never says he was blindfolded, so the taunt is odd.
steps.quote: Then they spat in his face and beat him with their fists, and some slapped him, saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who hit you?”

steps.point: Luke says they blindfolded him first.
steps.quote: Having blindfolded him, they struck him on the face and asked him, “Prophesy! Who is the one who struck you?”

steps.point: Luke's detail explains Matthew's taunt.

items.question: How would Matthew know what Herod said to his servants?

steps.point: Herod tells his servants that Jesus is John the Baptist raised.
steps.quote: …Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus, and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead.”

steps.point: Luke lists Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, among Jesus' followers.
steps.quote: …Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others who served them from their possessions.

steps.point: Luke also names Manaen, a companion of Herod, among the Antioch church.
steps.quote: …Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.

steps.point: Luke supplies plausible sources for a private conversation Matthew reports without explanation.

items.question: Why are James and John called 'Sons of Thunder'?

steps.point: Mark records the nickname but gives no reason.
steps.quote: James the son of Zebedee; and John, the brother of James, (whom he called Boanerges, which means, Sons of Thunder);

steps.point: Luke has James and John ask to call down fire on a Samaritan village.
steps.quote: …“Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?”

steps.point: The temperament Luke shows fits the nickname Mark records.

items.question: Where did the false witnesses get the 'destroy this temple' charge?

steps.point: At the trial, witnesses claim Jesus said he would destroy the temple. Mark records no such saying.
steps.quote: “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another made without hands.’”

steps.point: John, years earlier in the narrative, has Jesus say 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.'
steps.quote: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

steps.point: John supplies the saying; Mark supplies its garbled afterlife.

items.question: Why does Pilate ask whether Jesus is a Galilean?

steps.point: Pilate hears 'Galilee' and sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who governed it.
steps.quote: But when Pilate heard Galilee mentioned, he asked if the man was a Galilean. When he found out that he was in Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod…

steps.point: Luke had earlier set out exactly who ruled which region, so the jurisdictional move makes sense.
steps.quote: …Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene.

steps.point: Mark's parallel omits the Herod episode entirely; the jurisdiction detail is Luke's alone and fits known Roman practice.
steps.quote: Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” He answered, “So you say.” …Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate marveled.

items.question: Why could the disciples not even eat?

steps.point: So many were 'coming and going' that the disciples had no leisure to eat.
steps.quote: He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.

steps.point: John: Passover was near. Pilgrim traffic through Galilee toward Jerusalem peaked then.
steps.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.

steps.point: John's calendar note explains Mark's crowds.
